comparator.name: Politics, Psychology, Law and Economics
comparator.sourceNotes: The dated curriculum and adopted 2026–2027 Teaching and Examination Regulations provide seventeen shared core courses totalling 102 EC, nine Politics courses totalling 54 EC, a 12-EC thesis and 12 EC of electives. Politics remains the neutral first-listed major in the adopted curriculum, selected before UCR construction. Other majors are excluded. The public catalogue link leads to an earlier year; the dated 2026 catalogue and adopted regulations control this pathway.
components: The first year consists of ten compulsory 6-EC courses. Completing all 60 EC meets the first-year continuation threshold of 54 EC. What You Don’t Learn in School is an additional non-credit requirement in Years 1 and 2.
Economics for a Changing World I
Law and Behaviour requires the first-year Law, Justice and Morality course.
Economics for a Changing World II
Economics for a Changing World II requires Economics for a Changing World I.
Politics, Power and Governance II requires the first-year course. Its content centres on European integration, EU institutions and contemporary crises.
The Politics major requires Politics, Power and Governance I. The listed Politics courses form one major; courses from the other three majors are not added.
Skills and Research Methods for Political Science
The methods course develops quantitative political analysis and qualitative inquiry. Prior Introduction to Statistical Analysis is recommended and is completed in Year 1.
Conflict and Cooperation in Global Politics
Psychology and Society II requires Psychology and Society I. The course examines cultural and cross-cultural psychology.

Research Lab develops an interdisciplinary research proposal and offers methodological tutorial tracks. It is a separate compulsory course from the thesis; prior research-methods study is recommended.

The 12-EC thesis is an individual interdisciplinary research report, with an oral defence, in the second semester of Year 3. Entry requires 120 EC from academic core or major courses before that semester; electives do not count. Completing Years 1 and 2 and the first-semester major courses meets this threshold.

Twelve EC remain for electives, normally in the first semester of Year 3. Courses outside the designated PPLE electives require Examinations Board approval. An approved 6- or 12-EC internship may use this space; no internship or particular elective is assumed.

routeSelection.basis: The generic bachelor offers four disciplinary majors without a broad default. The adopted 2026–2027 curriculum lists Politics first. Retained this neutral official-order choice before UCR construction; no other major is included in the credit total.

core: Integrated analysis of social problems through politics, psychology, law and economics
Political power, governance, institutions, democracy and public policy
Human behaviour, social psychology, decision-making and behavioural approaches to public problems
Law, legal reasoning, justice, morality and the institutional foundations of society
Microeconomics, macroeconomics, behavioural economics and the economic dimensions of social challenges
Interdisciplinary research design, qualitative and quantitative methods, statistics and independent inquiry
adjacent: Behavioural public policy and the psychology of political and economic decisions
questions: How can political, psychological, legal and economic evidence be integrated to understand contemporary social problems?
How do human behaviour and decision-making shape public institutions and policy?
How do law, justice and economic institutions organise power, incentives and social outcomes?

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: develops academic writing, civic collaboration and reflective professional practice
introduces economic reasoning about markets, resources and government as a foundation for political-economic analysis
examines open-economy macroeconomic dynamics, goods, financial and labour markets, inflation, growth, and fiscal and monetary policy using formal models
examines microeconomic decisions, incentives and behavioural responses, supporting analysis of policy effects and political-economic choices
examines public intervention, equity, public goods, taxation, education, health and social insurance through policy models and research
develops econometric estimation, statistical tests and an empirical paper for analysing causal and predictive economic relationships relevant to policy
examines how biases, heuristics and framing change decisions through the integration of psychology and economics, including experiments
develops empirical design, measurement, sampling, statistics and a complete student data-collection project as research foundations for political inquiry
examines individual motivation, teams, leadership, power and organisational change, and develops research plans and a systematic literature review for organisational cases
develops bargaining, strategic choice, trust, framing and conflict management through negotiation simulations and an applied scenario project
develops data cleaning, transformation, visualisation and applied research in R, supporting empirical investigation of political evidence
develops statistical prediction, regression, classification, model evaluation and data analysis as computational complements to political research
introduces legal traditions, social justice and legal reasoning as foundations for studying political institutions and public power
examines human-rights law and philosophical claims, dignity, international protection and legal-political arguments

examines criminal liability, punishment, criminalisation and justice through legal cases and a criminology or organised-crime research proposal; it adds a legal perspective on security rather than replacing international-relations theory
examines international legal sources, states and institutions, force, conflict, human rights, economic and environmental law, and the political dimensions of law
compares constitutions, legislatures, executives, courts, judicial review, rights and administrative remedies as structures of public power
examines property, tort and contract rights and obligations across legal systems through case analysis, comparative research and simulated mediation
examines EU institutions, competences, supremacy, citizenship, free movement and judicial remedies through legal cases
develops moral reasoning and independent ethical arguments relevant to public responsibilities and competing political values
examines historical and contemporary political thought, authority, rights and society through original texts and normative argument
examines democracy, autocratisation, institutions, participation and political behaviour through empirical comparison and a research memo
examines competing international-relations theories, geopolitics, conflicts and global cooperation through case research and a UN simulation
examines EU institutions, integration, representation, legitimacy and policymaking, with an empirical research project on parliamentary amendments and interest influence
examines policy-making phases, policy actors and alternative analytical frameworks through a sugar-policy case and policy memos
examines conflict, inequality, identity and colonial legacies through interdisciplinary approaches to security, peacebuilding and justice, including a policy brief
develops qualitative interviewing, documentary inquiry, interpretation and reflexivity for social and political research
examines social movements, environmental justice and collective action through feminist, anticolonial and other perspectives
examines civil society, trust, solidarity, hegemony and social repair through theory and research on an organisation or initiative
introduces psychological and neural explanations of learning, personality, social influence and behaviour, supporting the psychological strand without substituting for social or political theory
examines social influence, group processes, prejudice, aggression and prosocial behaviour as psychological foundations for political interaction
develops experimental design and statistical analysis of multivariable models, categorical outcomes and latent constructs, with data-analysis papers and a research poster
examines youth radicalisation, risk, belonging, inclusive education and prevention through research-based teacher resources and a youth toolkit

alternatives.concept: Study justice and governance through public, private, constitutional, European and international law. Political thought, economics, social psychology, negotiation and qualitative inquiry support analysis of how institutions allocate rights, power and resources.

The closest option devotes more courses to economics, public policy and applied political psychology; the second gives more weight to computational and quantitative evaluation.

selection.assessment: The first plan is the closest integrated response across PPLE’s four disciplines and the selected Politics route. Behavioural public policy and law/justice/economic governance form separately evidenced priorities with concrete differences in courses, methods and emphasis. Every pair differs by at least four courses and thirty EC each way. Three is the maximum.

blocks: Politics, psychology, law, economics and methods
Both introduce economic choice, strategic interaction, firms, markets and the allocation of resources. UvA gives additional emphasis to institutional change, inequality and sustainability.
Both examine macroeconomic output, employment, inflation, growth, money and the IS-LM framework. UCR extends these foundations into open-economy analysis and policy.

Both develop regression-based empirical analysis and research reporting. UvA combines quantitative political analysis with qualitative methods; UCR concentrates on economic estimation, statistical tests and an empirical paper.
Both develop research questions, design, measurement, ethics and empirical inquiry through a student research project. UCR also provides introductory statistical analysis.
Both critically examine human-rights law, philosophical justifications, universality and rights in political and social contexts. UvA combines these perspectives in an integrative seminar.

Both examine the formal organisation of public power, state institutions and legal constraints on authority. UCR concentrates on constitutional and administrative law; UvA also analyses broader political power and decision-making processes.

Both examine competing normative theories, including consequentialism, deontology and virtue ethics, and apply moral arguments to social questions. UvA integrates these with legal philosophy and theories of justice.
Both examine political authority, rights, legitimacy and justice through classic and contemporary political thought and normative argument.
Both compare democracy, democratisation, authoritarian change, institutions and explanations of regime trajectories.
Both introduce international-relations theories and apply them to global power, conflict and cooperation involving states and other actors.
Both examine European integration, EU institutions, decision-making and legitimacy in relation to contemporary political challenges. UCR adds an empirical parliamentary project.
Both examine public policy, governance actors and alternative frameworks for understanding collective responses to social problems. UCR applies these through a policy case and memos.
Both examine causes and dynamics of conflict, international security and approaches to peace, including legal, political and social perspectives.

Both examine solidarity and the relationship between individual action and collective social life. UCR centres civil society, trust and social theory; UvA integrates psychological and economic explanations of cooperation.
Both examine social perception, attitudes, influence, prejudice, group processes and aggression through psychological research.

Both develop applied statistical analysis of group differences, relationships and multivariable models using real data and statistical software. UCR situates the methods in health and behavioural research.
Academic writing and argument occur across the UCR options, but no selected course provides the dedicated rhetorical analysis and public-speaking practice of this course.
The selected philosophy and methods courses support reasoning and research, but no dedicated philosophy-of-social-science course is selected.
The UCR legal, behavioural and negotiation courses provide complementary perspectives, but none centres the empirical mechanisms of legal compliance across the scope of Law and Behaviour.
The UCR courses address conflict and radicalisation, but no additional course is counted as the dedicated interdisciplinary security-research seminar.
Applied UCR projects support social engagement, but no additional course reproduces this reflective integrative seminar and its student interventions.
The UCR economics and institutional courses support political-economic inquiry, but none supplies this dedicated historical and international state–market relations sequence.
Political institutions and social psychology contribute to this theme elsewhere; no additional course centres the seminar’s specific democracy, truth, media and political-epistemology focus.
Social and organisational psychology are represented elsewhere. No selected course centres the cultural and cross-cultural psychology of this course.
UCR methods courses develop research designs and projects, but they are not counted again as the distinct interdisciplinary Research Lab.

Comparative politics and social psychology have stronger primary placements elsewhere. No additional selected course provides this dedicated survey of citizens’ and elites’ political attitudes and behaviour.
No compulsory individual interdisciplinary thesis is scheduled at UCR. Optional independent research appears separately outside the scheduled credits.
Open elective space remains unspecified; no particular elective or internship is invented.

notes.text: PPLE integrates four disciplines through a compulsory shared core, four integrative seminars, one formal major and an interdisciplinary thesis. UCR can combine substantial study in these disciplines with methods and applied projects. The course relationships shown are partial; the UCR options do not reproduce PPLE’s prescribed sequence or required thesis.

audience.programmeDescription: PPLE at the University of Amsterdam is an English-taught interdisciplinary bachelor in politics, psychology, law and economics. Students complete a shared core, four integrative seminars, one disciplinary major, electives and an interdisciplinary thesis. This example uses the Politics major.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR can combine substantial politics, social psychology, law, economics and research methods. Its options prioritise a broad four-field response, behavioural public policy and empirical evaluation, or law, justice and economic governance. PPLE provides a prescribed interdisciplinary sequence and required thesis; the course relationships shown are partial.
